description: We are a team of 5 people that are passionate about technology and storytelling. We like to work together and create games.
summary:
Zentra is a pixel-art story game that runs in the browser. Earth's cities are empty and full of radiation, and four survivors in an underground mission control fix up an old rocket. Their plan is to fly to the machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars, bring back parts, and learn from how they were built so they can make a rover that can search for other survivors.

    Players visit six real sites: Apollo 11's Eagle, Surveyor 3, the Apollo 15 rover, Mars Pathfinder with Sojourner, Opportunity and Ingenuity. At each one the crew talks about what the machine did and why it stayed behind. Then the player solves a puzzle based on a real task, such as aiming a laser at the mirror Apollo 11 left on the Moon or timing Pathfinder's airbags. Each puzzle ends with a short fact, and each machine unlocks a collectible card with real NASA photos.

    We answered the challenge by giving these machines a job in the story. Players learn the dates and numbers because the crew needs them to survive.
details:
ZENTRA is a short story game that runs in a web browser. Earth has been hit by a disaster and the cities are empty. Four survivors, Aurora, Clyde, Michael and Emily, set up a mission control in an old bunker and repair a rusty rocket. Their plan is to fly to the Moon and Mars, visit the machines NASA left there decades ago, and bring parts home. They'll study how those machines were built and use what they learn to make a new rover that can drive through the radiation on Earth and look for other survivors.

The player visits six real sites: Apollo 11's Eagle, Surveyor 3, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner, Opportunity and Ingenuity. Voyager 1 appears at the very end. Each site has a short puzzle based on what the spacecraft really did. The player aims a laser at the mirror Apollo 11 left on the Moon, puts Surveyor 3's two-bounce landing back in the right order, unfolds the lunar rover the way the Apollo 15 crew did, and times Pathfinder's airbags. After each puzzle comes a short "learn" note with the real facts behind it. Finding a spacecraft unlocks a collectible card with its stats, its story, NASA photos and an achievement.

We wanted to teach space history without it feeling like homework. Players remember a date like April 20, 1967 more easily once they've rebuilt Surveyor's landing themselves. The story also shows why old missions still matter. The radioisotope generator, the airbags and the helicopter each solve a problem the survivors have, so the player sees old hardware as a source of ideas for new designs. We hope players finish the game curious about these missions and go read more about them.

We built the game with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework, so it runs in any modern browser and needs no installation or special hardware. Each scene is a JSON file, so anyone on the team could write story and dialogue without touching the main engine. Each puzzle type (dial, order, wires, screws) is a small plugin. The visuals feature hand-drawn pixel art (characters, backgrounds, robotic spacecraft) at 480x270px, scaled. Sound effects come from Pixabay website. Every spacecraft fact comes from NASA sources: the NSSDCA spacecraft catalog, NASA Science mission pages and the NASA Image and Video Library. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help with code and to check the card texts against those sources.

On the way home the ship catches fire. The crew seals every part they collected inside a capsule and launches it toward Earth, where Emily is waiting to catch it. Then the ship is lost. Aurora drifts alone in her suit with 4% oxygen left when something golden floats out of the dark: Voyager 1. She remembers what Emily told them about it. It launched in 1977, flew past Jupiter and Saturn, and left the Sun's bubble in 2012. It carries a record with greetings in 55 languages, music, rain, laughter and pictures of Earth, with instructions on the cover so anyone who finds it can play it. The narrator then reminds the player that the real Voyager 1 is more than 24 billion kilometers away, so Aurora is seeing things. The real probe is still out there, still talking to Earth.

The creative part is the frame. Instead of a museum tour, the spacecraft are the clues in a survival story, and each visit gives the crew something they need. The ending tells the story of Voyager 1 and its Golden Record.

The last scene goes back to Emily in the bunker. The radio has been silent for hours. Then someone knocks on the door, and the game ends on one line: "Someone is out there."

Outside the story, players can open a garage to look back at every spacecraft they found, with its NASA photos and full story. An achievements screen shows what they have collected. Progress saves automatically, so the game can be played in short sessions. After completing a planet's chapter, it gets crossed with an X in the main menu. ZENTRA is free to play at https://zentra.earth and the code is public on GitHub.
